episode_title: The grief, loneliness, and burnout sweeping through the tech industry right now | Molly Graham
description_html:
Molly Graham is back for round two, and this one is even more powerful. Molly has spent more than 20 years helping organizations and the humans inside them navigate growth and change. She’s held leadership roles at Google, Facebook, Quip, and the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and is the host of TED’s WorkLife podcast (which she took over from Adam Grant). She also runs Glue Club, a leadership community for senior operators, and writes a popular newsletter called Lessons.

In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:

1. Why Molly’s famous “give away your Legos” career advice no longer holds true in an AI world

2. The grief, loneliness, and burnout sweeping through the tech industry right now

3. Why delegating to AI is fundamentally different from delegating to a human

4. The fear narrative around AI job displacement, and why it’s overblown

5. Which Legos you should never give to AI

6. What the best managers are doing right now

—

summary.overview: Molly Graham revisits her “Give Away Your Legos” career advice in the context of AI-driven change. She argues that the original principles still apply to rapid change, learning, and growth, but giving work to AI differs from giving it to a human: people retain responsibility, oversight, and the mental burden. The conversation addresses grief, loneliness, burnout, fear about jobs, management, and how to decide which work should remain distinctly human.

takeaways.heading: The original Lego metaphor
takeaways.detail: As companies grow, people naturally become attached to the projects, teams, and responsibilities they built. Graham’s advice is to give those “Legos” to someone else so you can grow into new work rather than becoming territorial or holding on to an old identity.

takeaways.heading: What still holds true
takeaways.detail: Change remains scary and difficult, and people should normalize the emotions that accompany it. Graham summarizes the enduring advice as making yourself irrelevant so you are ready for what comes next, learning rather than relying on what you already know, and leaning into change instead of standing still.

takeaways.heading: Grief and loneliness
takeaways.detail: AI is changing the substance of many jobs, especially engineering, where people may miss the flow state of writing and building code themselves. Smaller teams and more interaction with AI can also strip away collaboration and leave people feeling lonely; Graham argues leaders need to acknowledge that rather than insisting everyone be excited.

takeaways.heading: The fear narrative
takeaways.detail: Graham criticizes the message that AI is a superhuman employee that workers must train before it takes their jobs. She also questions layoffs branded as AI-driven, saying some are actually the result of companies hiring too many people, and argues that the current evidence does not establish that jobs are simply disappearing.

takeaways.heading: Jobs will be reinvented
takeaways.detail: Inspired by journalist Manoush Zomorodi’s career, Graham suggests asking, “What would you do if you believed your job was always going to exist? It was just going to look completely different every six years.” She believes people should help shape the next version of their profession instead of protecting its past form.

takeaways.heading: AI is not delegation
takeaways.detail: Giving a Lego to a human can genuinely remove responsibility; delegating to AI does not. AI currently behaves more like a junior or “lazy” intern that requires context, coaching, correction, and review, so people remain accountable for the final work and may end up managing many agents.

takeaways.heading: Productivity versus quality
takeaways.detail: The speakers distinguish producing more output from producing better work. They discuss AI slop, rewritten code, security concerns, and leaders copying AI-generated strategy documents, arguing that judgment, accountability, and a clear definition of “good” cannot simply be outsourced.

takeaways.heading: What not to give away
takeaways.detail: Graham makes an important qualification to her long-standing advice: some Legos should not be given to AI. Work involving human judgment, trust, vision, taste, quality standards, or responsibilities that the person does not yet understand well enough to evaluate should remain with humans.

takeaways.heading: Breaking down role boundaries
takeaways.detail: AI may reduce the walls between design, engineering, product management, and marketing. Graham encourages people to question what their role is fundamentally for and imagine new forms of work, while still respecting safeguards such as not sending unreviewed work into production.

takeaways.heading: Managers matter more
takeaways.detail: Managers and leaders are role models for how organizations use AI and define quality. Graham argues that management layers should not be casually eliminated, because managers help people feel seen, process change, maintain accountability, and navigate uncertainty; Lenny’s survey found the manager was the strongest lever for workplace happiness.

takeaways.heading: Practical posture
takeaways.detail: The speakers encourage asking, “Can AI help me with this?” while also asking whether the result is ambitious, good, and aligned with the world one wants to create. They recommend treating AI as an early-stage tool, making space to grieve what is lost, seeking communities for support, and remembering that the technology is still early enough for people to shape what comes next.

quotes.text: Your main job in the face of rapid growth and change is to make yourself irrelevant, because it is the only way that you can be prepared for whatever is coming next.
quotes.speaker: Molly Graham

quotes.text: What would you do if you believed your job was always going to exist? It was just going to look completely different every six years.
quotes.speaker: Molly Graham

quotes.text: Change sucks. It also can be awesome, but we don't have to be fluffy bunnies about this.
quotes.speaker: Molly Graham

quotes.text: The best way to give Legos away is to chuck them at their face and run in the other direction.
quotes.speaker: Molly Graham

quotes.text: AI needs the same coaching and training that a human does.
quotes.speaker: Molly Graham

quotes.text: Do not outsource that. You can enable it, you can amplify it to use your data, but don't outsource it to these weird robots that, you know, are effectively summer interns.
quotes.speaker: Molly Graham

quotes.text: We need to hold on to the definition of accountability and what good means.
